headings.text: Failure events in order of frequency

blocks.html:
Failure events in order of frequency

Many of these surface in logs first; see Audit logging & observability for where to look and what is normal versus suspicious.

Symptom Frequency Impact / end user symptom Log signal First action
OCSP stale Might happen once a week or so No mTLS path can be reached because no cert checking will pass via OCSP; MTLS_FAIL encountered in Deploy App UI healthcheck returns crlfail; CRL mtime past refresh interval Due to the age-based nature of OCSP actions, sometimes OCSP is not available during a 14-minut window of HH:00-HH:14. The solution is to wait until HH:15, then closing and reopening the browser before reconnection.In Kubernetes deployment we are getting rid of OCSP due to the time-based fragility.
Container crash loop in first startup Unusual but not unheard of When you are booting the instance, it won't start. Usually Keycloak or OpenLDAP might hang like this.If eg. TAK or MediaMTX hangs, the reason is always too little resources (RAM / CPU cores or a burstable CPU) assigned to the server. Reboot without volume removal does the job - unless the reason is too little resources assigned for the service.
Disk exhaustion Doesn't happen under normal conditions - can happen if you eg. run a lot data into TAKServer or Cryptpad. Usually the entire service goes down, to can't connect -level. No space left on device Clean logs/images, expand storage
Certificate chain broken Happens only if CA lifetime is expired. mTLS fails for all users ssl_verify_client errors; unknown CA Check cert and CA lifetime. If gone, there is no other option but to renew the service (docker compose down -v && docker compose up, and re-enroll users).
Container crash loop, during initially successful operations Should happen only in case of disk exhaustion, or resource exhaustion (too little CPU power or RAM assigned).If these are not the reasons, the reason is a developer problem, please contact us. Service unavailable Restarting (1) ... repeated; non-zero exit Read the container's logs for the root cause; verify its dependencies started

Guiding principle from the runbook: the product is meant not to fail, and when a local instance does misbehave, the expected remediation is to boot it down and back up (or, for a serious/critical issue, destroy and redeploy the instance).

Instance destruction is the expected fix for critical issues, because each instance is short-lived by design.

First-boot quirks (legacy local/dev)

OpenLDAP and the Keycloak init sometimes fail on the very first start. If so, just bring the composition up again. If switching between the rmlocal and rmdev development environments causes odd network issues, run down for one before starting the other.

A triage checklist

  1. Is everything running? docker compose ps (legacy) or kubectl get pods -A (k8s). Look for restart loops and non-Running/non-healthy states.
  2. What do the logs say? Start with rmapi, then rmnginx, then the failing component. Filter for ERROR/CRITICAL/fail.
  3. Are the dependencies healthy? Postgres, Keycloak, the CA, and OCSP underpin almost everything. Hit their health endpoints (see Audit logging & observability).
  4. Is it a security signal, not a fault? Cross-check against the compromise indicators before restarting — for a suspected compromise, preserve logs and do not restart.

Teardown — legacy (Docker Compose)

Stopping the stack without deleting data:
docker compose down
Destructive teardown — deletes persistent volumes (certificates, users, databases):

# !DO NOT DO! on an instance you want to keep —
# this removes the certificates etc. and you will have to add all users again
docker compose down -v

Use down -v only when you genuinely want a clean slate — for example resetting a dev environment, or before running the integration test suite (which expects a clean database). On a real instance, treat -v as "destroy this instance."

Teardown — Kubernetes

For a local kind instance, the project's task interface deletes the whole cluster (and therefore all instance data):

task down          # alias of cluster:delete — deletes the kind cluster
# equivalently:
task cluster:delete

Under the hood this runs kind delete cluster --name opendefense-kind, which destroys the cluster and all of its persistent volumes — the equivalent of down -v on the legacy stack.

On a shared/cloud cluster you usually do not want to delete the cluster. Instead remove the workload by deleting its namespace (this still destroys that instance's data):
kubectl delete namespace opendefense-system
